ctx.x: Henry. I want to get that straight. There's so many out.

Well, Merritt and Henry. No, no. Well, Merritt was a trumpet player. There's only two trombone players. George and... George came, you know, later. But Henry was the... There was two trombones that Ernest Giordina used. And that was Eddie Edwards and Henry Brunas. They were two of the kings down there. It was... You might have heard about Tom Brown, but they could never play with Giordina's band, because Giordina would play stuff out unorthodox. You understand? He played more. items.q: So Parenti would make his chorus and it would be great, and Barry would play his and it would be great.

ctx.x: Yeah. Yes. Yeah. But what I was getting at on that was that a lot of those arrangements that are from his collection that he left have a lot of string parts written now, is it that he would have just discarded these and not used this part as time went on when people didn't want so many strings. Like, for instance, they have cello parts and viola parts and so forth. What kind of orchestras would have used

all those parts? Would have been in the theaters and so forth? Mr. Robichaux was a very fine musician and a very fine gentleman. And he liked me. I mean we got along great. He was the one that I borrowed the orchestration of the panel often. And I concocted my own arrangement of it, you see. And you'd just have to take the parts. items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1969-12-04
items.q: No Johnny Detroit, no Tony Parenti, no, you know.

ctx.x: You want to get it going again? Okay.

Yeah, it's all right. I would rather it be known because I, truthfully, in spite of the fact that I thought he was more or less a mountainebank, now that's not a good thing to say, but he wasn't a musician he was talented to be, and he couldn't sing a lick, but he thought he could. But he was the finest gentleman you ever met. His whole heart was in music, and he liked me, and I turned on him. Only in this respect, that when he asked me for an interview, I said, what's the matter, you ran out of Negroes? Because…
Well, it may not have been his fault, you know. It may have been some pressure put on him by the publishers or something of the book.
